selection.warning: Counted by this project from the public DARWIN-1 catalogue of snapshot 1001 (z = 0.190). Halo mass is the Friends-of-Friends group mass `halo/mtot` (all particle species of the group, Msun/h divided by h = 0.674), not the M200,c of the paper's Fig. 10: the catalogue has no M200,c, so this relation is not comparable with M200-based ones. Stellar mass is the total stellar mass `sub/mstar` bound to the central galaxy. The catalogue has no central flag: the central is the galaxy (substructure with star particles) of largest stellar mass in the halo, as the finder's own paper (Kim et al. 2023, ApJ 951, 137) classifies the most massive galaxy of a halo as the central; Lee et al. 2026 say only 'the central galaxy, as identified by PGalF'. Taking the galaxy of largest total mass instead changes the central of 59 of 96593 halos with a galaxy and the bin medians by at most 0.001 dex. Only bins of 1/3 dex from 10^10.67 Msun upward, in which every halo hosts a galaxy (no selection on stellar mass), are kept: 9 bins with 10 or more centrals, 6402 centrals. Median and 16th to 84th percentile are taken from counts on a 0.05 dex grid of the stellar-to-halo mass ratio (the median is exact to about one grid cell). Cosmic variance of one box not included. Compared with the paper's Fig. 10, a raster image (its solid median line for the z = 0.19 panel read on axes calibrated from the tick marks and turned into a stellar-to-halo mass ratio, at 8 bin centres of this curve; internal check only): the paper's median ratio is higher than this curve's by 0.03 to 0.08 dex (median 0.07); the line is about 0.06 dex thick. The paper's halo mass is M200,c, which for the same halo is lower than its FoF mass, so the same galaxy has a higher ratio to M200,c than to the FoF mass: the offset has that sign, but this cause was not tested (the catalogue has no M200,c).

Black hole mass is `sub/mMBH`, the total mass of all black hole particles of the substructure (Msun/h divided by h = 0.674): a galaxy with several black hole particles counts their sum (0% of the hosts of 10^7 to 10^8 Msun and 99% of those above 10^10 Msun have two or more, on average 29.7 particles above 10^10 Msun). The catalogue does not give the mass of the most massive particle alone; it lies between the sum divided by the number of particles and the sum. Black holes are seeded at 5e4 Msun (Lee et al. 2026), so the median is close to the seed mass (10^4.70 Msun) at the lowest stellar masses. Median and 16th to 84th percentile are taken from counts on a 0.05 dex grid of black hole mass (the median is exact to about one grid cell). Cosmic variance of one box not included. Compared with the paper's Fig. 11, a raster image, lower panel, z = 0.19 (internal check only): the figure's grey DARWIN-1 dots and the same galaxies drawn as dots of the same size on the same calibrated axes, bins of 1/3 dex of stellar mass from 10^7 Msun (13 bins, pixels hidden under other symbols ignored in both): the 50th percentile of the dot pixels differs by +0.01 dex at the median over the bins, by at most 0.10 dex, and all of the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles agree within 0.2 dex in 12 of 13 bins. With only the galaxies that hold exactly one black hole particle, 5 bins have dots in the figure and no galaxy here (10^10.2 to 10^11.5 Msun), so the figure's population includes galaxies with several black hole particles; whether the paper sums their masses or takes the most massive one is not stated, and the sum reproduces the figure.
